newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-H-P CFO says inventory targeted.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-H-P CFO says inventory targeted.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Wayman said the company has been working to improve inventory management and to reduce sales channel inventories.

Wayman, speaking to investors at a Montgomery Securities investment conference, said the company has been pleased with progress in financial management, but he labeled inventory management as "the notable exception" to this.
"All in all we're very pleased with the progress that we've made," he said of the Palo Alto-based computing giant's ability to respond to changing market conditions.
"The notable exception would be our inventory management, where we've been struggling as we're dealing with how to deal with flat growth and long, complicated supply chains."
Wayman noted that in the retail channel, the company needed to build higher levels of inventory ahead of new product launches to meet subsequent customer demand.

"For example, when we introduce a new PC or printer, the expectation is that we should have about 200,000 products ready to ship at the time of the product announcement," he said, noting HP was seeking to improve management of this.
"While we haven't entirely turned the corner on inventory, we have slowed the growth significantly in the third quarter," he told investors.

"During that period, we have been working with our channel partners to reduce their inventory levels aswell, even if that resulted in cancelling outstanding orders in some instances," he said, without elaborating on the extent of cancellations.

Earlier, Weyman had noted the sharp drop in order growth in the third quarter to the end of July to eight percent from 35 percent a year earlier and 24 percent in the second quarter of fiscal 1996, saying management would in future be "pleased" with order percentage growth in the mid to high teens.
He said HP had decided that working with distribution channels was necessary to curb inventory problems.

"We believe that is the better course of action, to work with them to reduce their inventory and order backlog levels, than to incur the possibility of excessive price protection costs and inventory write-downs," he said.

While stating this would result in "a good outcome" eventually for return on assets and return on equity for the company, he added there was "...still lots of work to be done in the supply chain management as well as a few other areas."

Wayman highlighted HP's strategy in four key markets for its computing business which accounts for some 80 percent of HP revenues: enterprise computing for major organizations, interconnected workgroups, small businesses and the home.

He noted HP's strategy of developing high-end processors with Intel Corp to enable its most powerful machines to leapfrog a generation of computer technology, and Microsoft Corp's agreement that Windows NT will support this.
The senior executive also described how HP's recent efforts to build up marketing expertise to address the home market demonstrated HP's willingness to reinvent itself.
"Not so long ago, people used to say that we were the kind of company that would market sushi as cold, dead fish," he said, noting this was no longer a representative view.
